column1: # Introductions and summaries for stories. They are written by our editors and are NOT Scripture: the app shows
# them on their own cards, labelled "Introduction" or "Summary", never in Scripture type.
# Columns (TAB-separated): story slug, intro or summary, text. Keep them short, describe what the passage says,
# cite rather than quote, and avoid interpretations that belong to one tradition.
# Status: first drafts, awaiting editorial review in Story Studio.

column3: Matthew and Luke each tell how Jesus was born. Our editors have set their accounts side by side in time order, from the angel's visit to Mary to the wise men's journey. Each step shows one Gospel's own words; the first step lets you compare the two family lines.

An angel tells Mary she will bear a son, and Joseph is told in a dream to take Mary as his wife. Jesus is born in Bethlehem and laid in a manger. Angels announce the birth to shepherds, and wise men from the east follow a star to worship the child.
John the Baptist preaches in the wilderness of Judaea, calling people to repent and be baptized in the Jordan. Each Gospel links him with the "voice crying in the wilderness" of Isaiah 40.
Jesus comes to John at the Jordan to be baptized. As he comes up out of the water, the Spirit descends like a dove and a voice speaks from heaven. Three Gospels tell it; switch tabs to read each one.
After his baptism Jesus spends forty days in the wilderness and is tempted by the devil. Matthew and Luke record three temptations and Jesus' answers from Deuteronomy; Mark tells it in two verses.

Sick of the palsy means paralysed. Friends bring the man to Jesus, in Mark and Luke by letting him down through the roof. Jesus first tells him his sins are forgiven, which troubles the scribes, and then tells him to rise and walk.

Jesus calls a tax collector sitting at his tax booth (the "receipt of custom"), named Matthew in Matthew's Gospel and Levi in Mark and Luke. Jesus then eats with tax collectors and "sinners", and explains why to those who object.
A great storm rises while Jesus and his disciples cross the Sea of Galilee, and Jesus is asleep in the boat. Three Gospels tell what happened when they woke him.

The disciples wake Jesus in fear. He rebukes the wind and the sea and there is a great calm. He asks them about their faith, and they ask one another what kind of man this is, that even the wind and the sea obey him.

On the far shore of the Sea of Galilee Jesus meets a man (two men in Matthew's account) possessed by many devils, who lives among the tombs. The devils call themselves Legion. KJV "devils" are evil spirits.

Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, begs Jesus to come to his dying daughter. On the way, a woman who has been ill for twelve years touches the hem of his garment. The Gospels tell the two events woven together.

This is the only miracle of Jesus told in all four Gospels. A great crowd has followed him to a remote place, and there is little food. Switch tabs to read Matthew, Mark, Luke or John; each keeps its own details.

With five loaves and two fishes Jesus gives thanks, and the disciples hand out the food. About five thousand men, besides women and children in Matthew's account, eat and are filled, and twelve baskets of fragments are gathered up.

After the feeding of the five thousand the disciples set out by boat while Jesus stays to pray. In the night he comes to them walking on the sea. Matthew alone tells of Peter stepping out of the boat.
Near Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is, and then who they say he is. Peter answers for them.

Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain. There he is transfigured, which means his appearance is changed: his face and clothes shine with light. Moses and Elijah (Elias in the KJV) appear and talk with him.

A bright cloud overshadows them and a voice says, "This is my beloved Son... hear ye him." The disciples fall on their faces. When they look up they see Jesus only, and he tells them to tell no one until he has risen from the dead.
A man asks Jesus what he must do to have eternal life. Matthew says he was young, Luke says he was a ruler, and all three say he had great possessions.

As Jesus leaves Jericho on his way to Jerusalem, blind men by the roadside cry out to him as the "son of David". Mark names one of them: Bartimaeus. Matthew tells of two men; Luke places the healing as Jesus comes near the city.

Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey (an "ass" or "colt" in the KJV) as crowds spread garments and branches on the road and shout "Hosanna". All four Gospels tell it. Matthew and John point to Zechariah 9:9.

The disciples bring the animal, and Jesus rides into the city while the crowds praise God. In Matthew the whole city is stirred and asks who this is; in Luke some Pharisees tell Jesus to rebuke his disciples, and he answers that if they were silent, the stones would cry out.

In Jerusalem Jesus drives out those who bought and sold in the temple and overturns the tables of the moneychangers, saying the house of prayer had been made a den of thieves. John tells of a temple cleansing at the start of Jesus' ministry; it is linked under related passages.

Jesus tells of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to look for one that is lost. Luke sets it among three parables about lost things told to Pharisees and scribes who complained that Jesus received sinners; Matthew sets it in teaching about "these little ones".

Shortly before the Passover, at Bethany, a woman pours very costly ointment on Jesus. Some object to the waste. John names her as Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus. Luke 7 tells of a different anointing.

On the night he is betrayed, Jesus eats the Passover meal with the twelve. He says one of them will betray him, and he gives them bread and the cup. Matthew, Mark and Luke each tell it in their own words.

Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it to the disciples, saying "this is my body", and then the cup, "my blood of the new testament". They sing a hymn and go out to the mount of Olives. In Luke, Jesus also tells Peter that he will deny him three times.
After the supper Jesus goes with his disciples to a place called Gethsemane on the mount of Olives. He prays in great sorrow, while the disciples he asked to watch with him fall asleep.

Judas arrives with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests and identifies Jesus. A disciple strikes the high priest's servant with a sword; John names the disciple as Peter and the servant as Malchus.
While Jesus is questioned at the high priest's house, Peter waits in the courtyard. Three times he is asked whether he was with Jesus, and three times he denies it. Then the cock crows.

The chief priests bring Jesus to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate questions him, offers to release a prisoner for the feast, and the crowd asks for Barabbas. John's account records the longest conversation between Jesus and Pilate.

Jesus is mocked by soldiers, led out to Golgotha, "the place of a skull", and crucified between two others. All four Gospels tell it, each with its own words from the cross. Read one account at a time with the tabs.

Jesus is crucified, and a title on the cross calls him King of the Jews. Darkness covers the land in the first three Gospels. Jesus dies, and in Matthew, Mark and Luke the veil of the temple is torn in two. A centurion who sees it speaks of him as righteous or as the Son of God.
Joseph of Arimathaea, a rich man and a disciple, asks Pilate for the body of Jesus and lays it in a new tomb cut in rock. John adds that Nicodemus brought spices. Women watch where he is laid.
Early on the first day of the week, women come to the tomb and find the stone rolled away. Each Gospel tells the morning in its own way: switch tabs to read Matthew, Mark, Luke or John.

The tomb is empty. Angels tell the women that Jesus is risen, as he said. In Matthew the women meet Jesus on the way; in John, Mary Magdalene meets him in the garden and mistakes him for the gardener until he speaks her name.

On the evening of the resurrection Jesus stands among his disciples and says "Peace be unto you". He shows them his hands, and his feet in Luke and his side in John. Luke and John each record the meeting.
The Philistines defeat Israel on mount Gilboa. Saul's sons, Jonathan among them, are killed, and Saul himself dies. First Samuel and First Chronicles both record it; Chronicles adds why Saul died.

David brings the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem with music and dancing. On the way, Uzzah touches the ark and dies, and David waits three months before trying again. Chronicles gives the fuller account, with the Levites and their songs.
David wants to build a house for God. Through the prophet Nathan, God answers that he will build David a house instead: a lasting kingdom through David's offspring. David responds with a prayer.

David orders a count of the fighting men of Israel, and then knows he has sinned. A plague follows, which stops at the threshing floor of Araunah (called Ornan in Chronicles), where David builds an altar.
God appears to the young King Solomon in a dream at Gibeon and says, "Ask what I shall give thee." Solomon asks for an understanding heart to judge the people.
Solomon builds the house of the Lord in Jerusalem with cedar from Lebanon and craftsmen from Tyre. Kings and Chronicles both describe the work and its furnishings in detail.
The ark is brought into the finished temple and the glory of the Lord fills the house. Solomon blesses the people and prays a long prayer of dedication.
The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon's fame and comes to test him with hard questions. She sees his wisdom and his court, and blesses the Lord his God.

After Solomon's death, the people ask his son Rehoboam to lighten their burdens. He takes the advice of the young men instead of the old, and ten tribes turn to Jeroboam. The kingdom divides into Israel in the north and Judah in the south.
When Athaliah seizes the throne of Judah and kills the royal heirs, the infant Joash is hidden in the temple for six years. The priest Jehoiada then crowns him king. Joash later repairs the temple.
Hezekiah, king of Judah, removes the high places and trusts in the Lord. Chronicles tells at length how he reopened and cleansed the temple and kept a great Passover.

Sennacherib, king of Assyria, sends his officers to Jerusalem to demand surrender. Hezekiah takes the threatening letter to the temple and prays, and the prophet Isaiah brings God's answer. The same events are told in Kings, Chronicles and Isaiah.

Hezekiah is sick to the point of death. He prays, and Isaiah tells him that fifteen years will be added to his life, with the sign of the shadow going back on the sundial. Afterwards envoys from Babylon visit, and Hezekiah shows them all his treasures.

Manasseh reigns longer than any other king of Judah and leads the people into the worship of other gods. Kings records his evil and its consequences; Chronicles adds that he was taken to Babylon in chains, humbled himself, and prayed.
During repairs to the temple, the priest Hilkiah finds the book of the law. When it is read to King Josiah he tears his clothes, and he leads Judah in renewing the covenant and keeping the Passover.
Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieges Jerusalem. The city falls, the temple is burned, and the people are carried away into exile. Kings and Jeremiah both record it.
The Bible opens with God creating the heavens and the earth. Over six days God speaks and it is so, and on the seventh day God rests.

God creates light, sky, sea and land, plants, the sun, moon and stars, creatures of sea, air and land, and finally humankind in his own image, male and female. God sees everything he has made, and it is very good.
The earth is filled with violence, but Noah finds grace in the eyes of the Lord. God tells him to build an ark and bring his family and the animals into it.
God tells Abraham to take his son Isaac, whom he loves, to a mountain in the land of Moriah and offer him there. This is one of the most searching stories in Genesis.
Years after his brothers sold him into slavery, Joseph is ruler over Egypt. His brothers stand before him without knowing who he is, until he can no longer hold back.
Israel has left Egypt, but Pharaoh's army pursues them to the edge of the sea. Moses tells the people to stand still and see the salvation of the Lord.

Moses stretches out his hand, a strong east wind blows all night, and Israel crosses on dry ground. When the Egyptians follow, the waters return. The people fear the Lord and believe him and his servant Moses.
The Philistine champion Goliath challenges Israel's army for forty days. David, a young shepherd bringing food to his brothers, hears the challenge.
David refuses Saul's armour and goes out with his sling and five smooth stones, saying the battle is the Lord's. He strikes Goliath with a stone and the Philistines flee.
Officials of King Darius trick him into making a law that no one may pray to any god or man but the king for thirty days. Daniel keeps praying three times a day at his open window.
Daniel is thrown into the den of lions. In the morning the king finds him unhurt: God sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths. Darius decrees that all should fear the God of Daniel.
God tells the prophet Jonah to go to the great city of Nineveh and cry against it. Jonah sets off by ship in the opposite direction.
Prodigal means wasteful. Jesus tells of a younger son who takes his inheritance and wastes it in a far country, and of the father and elder brother he left behind.

In need, the son comes to himself and goes home to confess. His father sees him a great way off, runs to him and celebrates his return. The elder brother is angry, and the father tells him, "this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found."
A lawyer asks Jesus, "Who is my neighbour?" Jesus answers with a story about a man beaten by robbers, the people who pass him by, and a Samaritan who stops.
At the feast of Pentecost the disciples are gathered together when a sound like a rushing mighty wind fills the house, and they begin to speak in other languages. Peter then speaks to the crowd.
Saul of Tarsus is on the road to Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus when a light from heaven shines around him and a voice speaks. Saul is later known as Paul.
The serpent questions what God said to the woman in the garden of Eden. She and the man eat the fruit of the tree God told them not to eat, and everything changes.
Adam and Eve's sons bring offerings to the Lord. God accepts Abel's offering and not Cain's, and Cain's anger leads to the first murder.
The whole earth has one language. People on the plain of Shinar set out to build a city and a tower reaching to heaven, to make a name for themselves.
God tells Abram to leave his country and his father's house for a land God will show him, and promises to make of him a great nation through whom all families of the earth will be blessed.
Moses is keeping sheep near Horeb, the mountain of God, when he sees a bush that burns but is not consumed. God calls to him from the bush.
Pharaoh refuses to let Israel go. Ten plagues follow, from water turned to blood to the death of the firstborn. These chapters tell the first nine and the warning of the tenth.
Before the last plague, God tells each household in Israel to kill a lamb and put its blood on the doorposts, and to eat the meal ready to leave. Israel is told to keep this day as a feast for ever.
At mount Sinai, with thunder and lightning on the mountain, God speaks the ten commandments to Israel.
While Moses is on the mountain, the people ask Aaron to make them gods. He makes a calf of gold, and Moses comes down to find them worshipping it.
Joshua meets the captain of the Lord's host near Jericho. Israel is told to march around the shut-up city once a day for six days, and seven times on the seventh.
Ruth, a Moabite widow, goes to glean leftover grain in the fields to provide for her mother-in-law Naomi. She happens to come to the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi's late husband.
The boy Samuel serves under the priest Eli at Shiloh. One night he hears a voice calling his name, and thinks it is Eli.
After three years of drought, Elijah challenges the prophets of Baal to a contest on mount Carmel: each side will call on its god, and "the God that answereth by fire, let him be God."
King Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image and commands everyone to bow to it. Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego refuse.
At King Belshazzar's feast, using the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem, the fingers of a man's hand appear and write on the wall. Daniel is called to read it.
Psalm 23, a psalm of David, pictures the Lord as a shepherd who provides, leads and comforts, and as a host who prepares a table.
In a vision, Ezekiel is set down in a valley full of very dry bones. God asks him, "Son of man, can these bones live?"
Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up a mountain and teaches his disciples. These three chapters include the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer and the parable of the wise and foolish builders.
Jesus, his mother and his disciples are at a wedding in Cana of Galilee when the wine runs out. John calls what happens next the beginning of Jesus' miracles.
Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler of the Jews, comes to Jesus by night. Jesus tells him that a man must be born again to see the kingdom of God.
Tired from his journey, Jesus sits by Jacob's well in Samaria and asks a woman for a drink. Jews and Samaritans did not usually have dealings with one another.
Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Mary and Martha, is sick, but Jesus waits two days before going to him. By the time he arrives, Lazarus has been in the grave four days.
Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector in Jericho, is too short to see Jesus over the crowd, so he climbs a sycomore tree.
On the day of the resurrection two disciples walk to a village called Emmaus, talking about all that has happened. Jesus draws near and walks with them, but they do not recognise him.
Thomas was not with the other disciples when Jesus appeared to them, and says he will not believe unless he sees and touches the wounds. Eight days later Jesus comes again.
By the Sea of Tiberias, after breakfast with his disciples, Jesus asks Peter three times, "lovest thou me?"
The eleven disciples meet the risen Jesus on a mountain in Galilee, where he sends them to make disciples of all nations.
Before the feast of the Passover, Jesus rises from supper, takes a towel and washes his disciples' feet. Peter at first refuses.
Jesus tells of a sower whose seed falls on four kinds of ground, and then explains the parable to his disciples.
Haman has obtained a decree to destroy the Jews of the Persian empire. Mordecai urges Queen Esther to go to the king, though to approach him unsummoned could cost her life.
Naaman, commander of the army of Syria, has leprosy. A captive Israelite girl tells of a prophet in Samaria who could heal him, and the prophet Elisha sends him to wash in the Jordan seven times.
Paul writes to the church at Corinth about spiritual gifts, the church as one body with many members, and, in chapter 13, about charity, which in the KJV means love.

column1: # Introductions for the remaining stories (one per story).

column3: The second chapter of Genesis tells of creation again, this time close up: the Lord God forms the man from the dust of the ground, plants a garden in Eden, and makes the woman from the man's side.

Two family lines follow the first murder: Cain's descendants, among them the first city-builder, musicians and metalworkers, and the line of Seth from Adam to Noah. Methuselah and Enoch, who "walked with God", appear here.
The earth is filled with wickedness, and the Lord is grieved that he made man. Only Noah finds grace in his eyes. "Repented" in the KJV here means that God was sorry or grieved.

The waters rise over the earth for many days and every living thing outside the ark perishes. Then God remembers Noah, the waters go down, the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat, and a dove is sent out.
After the flood Noah builds an altar. God promises never again to destroy the earth by a flood, and sets his bow in the cloud as the sign of the covenant.
Noah plants a vineyard and becomes drunk. How his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth respond leads to Noah's blessing and his curse on Canaan, Ham's son.
Famine drives Abram to Egypt. Afraid for his life, he says that Sarai his wife is his sister, and Pharaoh takes her into his house until the Lord sends plagues.
Abram and his nephew Lot part ways, and Lot settles near Sodom. When kings capture Lot in a war, Abram rescues him and is blessed by Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the most high God.
Abram is still childless. God tells him to look at the stars and count them, "so shall thy seed be", and Abram believes the Lord. God then makes a covenant with him in a solemn ceremony.
Sarai, still without children, gives her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abram. Hagar conceives and flees from Sarai's harsh treatment, and the angel of the Lord meets her by a spring in the wilderness.
God renames Abram as Abraham and Sarai as Sarah, promises that Sarah will bear a son, and gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant. Abraham laughs at the thought of a child at his age.
Three men visit Abraham's tent at Mamre in the heat of the day, and he hurries to welcome them. One of them says Sarah will have a son, and Sarah, listening at the tent door, laughs.
The Lord tells Abraham that the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great. Abraham asks whether he will spare the city for fifty righteous people, then forty-five, down to ten.
Two angels come to Sodom, where Lot takes them in and the men of the city surround his house. At dawn the angels lead Lot's family out, fire and brimstone fall, and Lot's wife looks back.
After Sodom's destruction, Lot and his two daughters live in a cave. This short and troubling account explains the origins of the Moabites and the Ammonites.
In Gerar, Abraham again says that Sarah is his sister, and King Abimelech takes her. God warns Abimelech in a dream, and he returns Sarah to Abraham.
The Lord does as he promised, and Sarah bears Abraham a son in his old age. They name him Isaac, which means laughter, and Sarah says, "God hath made me to laugh".
At the feast for Isaac's weaning, Sarah sees Ishmael mocking and asks Abraham to send him and Hagar away. In the wilderness of Beersheba the water runs out, and God hears the boy's voice.
Sarah dies at Hebron aged 127. Abraham, a stranger in the land, buys the cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite as a burying place, his first owned ground in Canaan.
Abraham sends his servant to his family's homeland to find a wife for Isaac. At the well, the servant prays for a sign, and Rebekah offers water for him and his camels.
Rebekah's twins struggle within her, and she is told that the elder will serve the younger. Years later Esau, hungry from the field, sells his birthright to Jacob for bread and lentil pottage.
During a famine Isaac lives in Gerar and the Lord renews to him the promises made to Abraham. Isaac's wells cause disputes with the Philistine herdsmen until he digs one at Rehoboth, "room".
Isaac, old and blind, plans to bless Esau. Rebekah and Jacob use goatskins and Esau's clothes to deceive him, and Jacob receives the blessing instead. Esau vows to kill his brother.
Fleeing from Esau, Jacob sleeps on the way with a stone for a pillow. He dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven with angels ascending and descending, and the Lord renews his promise.
At a well in Haran, Jacob meets Rachel, daughter of his uncle Laban. He serves seven years for her, but on the wedding night Laban gives him Leah instead.
Leah, Rachel and their maids Bilhah and Zilpah bear Jacob eleven sons and a daughter. Each name records the mother's feelings, ending with Rachel's son Joseph.
Jacob's flocks grow while Laban keeps changing his wages. Jacob leaves secretly for Canaan with his family, Laban pursues him, and they make a covenant at a heap of stones.
Jacob prepares to meet Esau and prays for deliverance. At the ford Jabbok a man wrestles with him until daybreak. Jacob is given the name Israel and calls the place Peniel.
Jacob bows seven times as he approaches Esau, but Esau runs to meet him, embraces him and weeps. The brothers part in peace.
Jacob's daughter Dinah is taken and humbled by Shechem, a local prince. Her brothers Simeon and Levi take a violent revenge on the city, and Jacob rebukes them.
God sends Jacob back to Bethel, where he puts away foreign gods and builds an altar. On the road to Bethlehem, Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, and Isaac dies at Hebron.

Jacob loves Joseph more than his other sons and gives him a coat of many colours. Joseph's dreams of his family bowing to him deepen his brothers' hatred, and they sell him to traders bound for Egypt.
An interruption in Joseph's story: Judah fails to keep his promise to his widowed daughter-in-law Tamar, and she takes matters into her own hands. Her son Pharez is later an ancestor of David.
In Egypt, Joseph serves in the house of Potiphar, and the Lord prospers everything he does. Potiphar's wife tries to seduce him, and when he refuses she accuses him falsely. He is put in prison.
In prison, Pharaoh's butler and baker each have a dream. Joseph says that interpretations belong to God and explains both dreams, which come true, but the butler forgets him.
Pharaoh dreams of seven fat and seven lean cattle, and no one can explain it. The butler remembers Joseph, who foretells seven years of plenty and seven of famine and is made ruler over Egypt.
Famine reaches Canaan, and Jacob sends ten sons to buy grain in Egypt. Joseph recognises his brothers, though they do not recognise him, and he accuses them of being spies.
The grain runs out and the brothers must return to Egypt with Benjamin, Jacob's youngest son. Joseph welcomes them to a meal in his house and has to leave the room to weep.
Joseph has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack, and Benjamin is accused of theft. Judah offers to stay as a slave in his place, for their father's sake.
God tells Jacob not to fear going down to Egypt. Jacob's family of seventy settles in the land of Goshen, Jacob blesses Pharaoh, and Joseph manages Egypt through the famine.
Jacob, near death, adopts Joseph's two sons as his own. He crosses his hands to put his right hand on the younger, Ephraim, and his left on the elder, Manasseh.
Jacob gathers his twelve sons and speaks to each of them in poetry about what will befall them. Judah is told that the sceptre shall not depart from him.
Jacob is buried in Canaan with great mourning. His sons fear Joseph's revenge, but Joseph answers, "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." Joseph dies in Egypt.
A new king arises who does not know Joseph. Fearing Israel's growing numbers, he makes them slaves and orders the Hebrew midwives to kill the baby boys, but the midwives fear God.
A Levite mother hides her baby boy and then sets him in an ark of bulrushes on the Nile. Pharaoh's daughter finds him, and his sister arranges for his own mother to nurse him.
Grown up, Moses kills an Egyptian he sees beating a Hebrew, and he flees to Midian. There he helps the daughters of a priest at a well, marries Zipporah, and God hears Israel's groaning.
Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel go. Pharaoh answers, "Who is the LORD?" and makes their work harder, and the people blame Moses. God renews his promise, and Aaron's rod becomes a serpent.
At midnight the firstborn of Egypt die, and Pharaoh at last tells Israel to go. The people leave in haste with their unleavened dough, after 430 years in Egypt.
God claims every firstborn as his, and Moses gives instructions for remembering the exodus. God leads the people the long way, by a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night.
On the far side of the sea, Moses and Israel sing to the Lord, "he hath triumphed gloriously". Miriam the prophetess takes a timbrel and the women answer her with dancing.
Three days into the wilderness the people find only bitter water at Marah, and they murmur. The Lord shows Moses a tree which makes the water sweet, and they come to Elim with its twelve wells.
The hungry people complain. God sends quails in the evening and, in the morning, manna, a small round thing on the ground. Each day's gathering is enough, with a double portion before the sabbath.
At Rephidim there is no water and the people quarrel with Moses. God tells him to strike the rock in Horeb, and water comes out. The place is named Massah and Meribah.
Amalek attacks Israel at Rephidim. Joshua leads the fight while Moses holds up his hands on the hilltop, with Aaron and Hur supporting them until sunset.
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, sees Moses judging the people from morning to evening. He advises him to appoint able men as rulers over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.
Israel camps before mount Sinai. God offers to make them "a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation", and comes down on the mountain in fire, smoke, thunder and the sound of a trumpet.
The people promise to do all the Lord has said. Moses sprinkles the blood of the covenant, and the elders see the God of Israel. Moses goes up into the cloud for forty days and nights.
On the mountain God gives Moses the pattern for the tabernacle, a portable sanctuary: the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altar, the priests' garments and the craftsmen Bezaleel and Aholiab.
After the golden calf, Moses pleads for the people and asks to see God's glory. God passes by, proclaiming his name, "merciful and gracious", and renews the covenant on new tables of stone.
The people bring so many offerings that Moses has to stop them. The craftsmen make everything as commanded, the tabernacle is set up, and the glory of the Lord fills it.
Moses washes, clothes and anoints Aaron and his sons as priests before the whole congregation, and they stay at the door of the tabernacle for seven days of consecration.
On the eighth day Aaron offers the first sacrifices. He blesses the people, the glory of the Lord appears, and fire comes out from before the Lord to consume the offering.
Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offer "strange fire" that the Lord had not commanded, and fire from the Lord devours them. Aaron holds his peace.
God gives instructions for the yearly Day of Atonement. The high priest enters the holy place within the veil, and one goat is offered while the other, the scapegoat, is sent into the wilderness.

These chapters, sometimes called the Holiness Code, teach Israel to be holy "for I the LORD your God am holy". They include "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself", the feasts, the jubilee, and blessings and warnings.
A year after leaving Egypt, Moses counts the men of Israel able to go to war, tribe by tribe. The tribes are arranged around the tabernacle, and the Levites are given its care.
When the tabernacle is set up, the leader of each tribe brings an identical offering on twelve successive days. Moses then hears the voice speaking from above the mercy seat.
The cloud covers the tabernacle, and Israel moves or stays as it moves or stays. Silver trumpets are made, and Israel sets out from Sinai with the ark going before them.
The people complain about the manna and long for the fish and vegetables of Egypt. Moses feels the burden is too heavy, God shares his spirit with seventy elders, and quails arrive in great numbers.
Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses, asking whether the Lord has spoken only by him. God defends Moses, "the man Moses was very meek", and Miriam is struck with leprosy for seven days.
Moses sends twelve men to spy out Canaan. They bring back a cluster of grapes carried on a pole and report a land flowing with milk and honey, but ten of them say the people there are too strong.
The people weep all night and want to return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb plead with them to trust the Lord. God declares that this generation will wander forty years in the wilderness.
Korah, Dathan and Abiram lead a rebellion against Moses and Aaron. The ground opens and swallows the leaders, and Aaron stands between the dead and the living to stop a plague.
To settle who God has chosen as priest, a rod from each tribe is laid in the tabernacle. Overnight Aaron's rod buds, blossoms and yields almonds.
Miriam dies, and at Kadesh there is no water. God tells Moses to speak to the rock, but Moses strikes it twice. Water flows, but God says Moses and Aaron will not bring Israel into the land.
At mount Hor, Moses strips Aaron of his priestly garments and puts them on his son Eleazar. Aaron dies on the mountain, and Israel mourns him thirty days.

The people speak against God and Moses, and fiery serpents bite them. God tells Moses to make a serpent of brass and set it on a pole, and whoever looks at it lives. Jesus refers to this in John 3:14.
Balak, king of Moab, hires the prophet Balaam to curse Israel. On the way Balaam's ass sees the angel of the Lord before he does. Each time Balaam opens his mouth, he blesses Israel instead.
At Shittim the men of Israel join in the worship of Baal-peor with Moabite women, and a plague breaks out. Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, acts zealously and the plague is stayed.
Zelophehad has died with no sons. His five daughters ask for their father's inheritance, Moses brings their case to the Lord, and God says they speak right.

God tells Moses to view the land from the mountain, for he will not enter it. Moses asks God to set a man over the people, "that the congregation of the LORD be not as sheep which have no shepherd". Joshua is chosen.
Israel goes to war against Midian after the sin at Peor. The chapter also gives rules for purification after battle and for dividing the spoil.
The tribes of Reuben and Gad, rich in cattle, ask to settle in the land east of the Jordan. Moses agrees on condition that their men cross over and fight alongside their brothers first.
Deuteronomy opens with Moses speaking to Israel on the plains of Moab. He recalls their journey from Horeb, the refusal at Kadesh, and the victories over Sihon and Og.
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD. Moses calls Israel to love God with all their heart, soul and might, and to teach his words to their children.
Moses sets before Israel blessing and cursing, life and death. Ending with a call to choose life, these chapters lay out what faithfulness and unfaithfulness to the covenant will bring.
Moses, now 120, tells Israel he will not cross the Jordan. He charges Joshua to be strong and of a good courage, and writes the law and gives it to the priests to be read every seven years.
Moses speaks a song in the ears of all Israel, a poem that praises God as the Rock and warns Israel of turning away. Afterwards God tells Moses to climb mount Nebo.
Before his death, Moses blesses each tribe of Israel in turn. He ends, "The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms."
Moses climbs mount Nebo, and the Lord shows him the whole land. Moses dies there and God buries him, and no man knows his grave. Israel mourns thirty days, and Joshua leads them.
After Moses' death the Lord tells Joshua to lead Israel over the Jordan. Three times he is told to "be strong and of a good courage", and to keep the book of the law.

Joshua sends two spies to Jericho, and Rahab hides them on her roof. She says the people's hearts have melted for fear of Israel's God, and she asks for her family's safety. A scarlet cord marks her house.
The priests carry the ark into the Jordan at flood season, and the waters stand up in a heap. Israel crosses on dry ground, and twelve stones from the river are set up as a memorial.
At Gilgal, the men born in the wilderness are circumcised and Israel keeps the Passover. The next day they eat the produce of the land, and the manna stops.
Israel is defeated at the small town of Ai. Joshua falls on his face before the ark, and the cause is traced to Achan, who took things from Jericho that were devoted to God.
Joshua takes Ai by an ambush. Afterwards he builds an altar on mount Ebal and reads all the words of the law to the people, as Moses had commanded.
The Gibeonites pretend to come from a far country, with old sacks and mouldy bread, and Israel makes a treaty with them without asking counsel of the Lord.
Five Amorite kings attack Gibeon, and Joshua comes to its defence. Great hailstones fall, and at Joshua's word the sun stands still over Gibeon. Israel then takes the southern cities.
The kings of the north gather at the waters of Merom with horses and chariots "as the sand that is upon the sea shore". Joshua defeats them and takes Hazor.

The land is divided among the tribes by lot. Caleb receives Hebron at eighty-five, cities of refuge are set apart, and the Levites receive cities. These chapters close with "there failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken".
The tribes east of the Jordan go home and build a great altar by the river. The other tribes prepare for war, fearing rebellion, until they learn it is a witness and not an altar for sacrifice.
Old Joshua gathers Israel at Shechem and recounts what God has done. He says, "choose you this day whom ye will serve... as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."

After Joshua's death the tribes fail to drive out the peoples of the land. A new generation arises that does not know the Lord, setting up the cycle of the book of Judges: sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance.
Israel serves other gods and falls under the king of Mesopotamia for eight years. When they cry to the Lord, the Spirit of the Lord comes on Othniel, Caleb's nephew, who delivers them.
Israel serves Eglon, king of Moab. Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, brings tribute to Eglon, asks for a private audience, and kills him with a hidden dagger.
A single verse: Shamgar the son of Anath kills six hundred Philistines with an ox goad, and he also delivers Israel.

Under Jabin of Canaan and his captain Sisera, Israel is oppressed for twenty years. Deborah, a prophetess judging Israel, sends Barak to battle. Sisera flees and dies by the hand of Jael. Chapter 5 is Deborah's song.

Midian raids Israel's crops every year. The angel of the Lord finds Gideon threshing wheat in hiding and calls him a mighty man of valour. Gideon tears down his father's altar to Baal and asks for signs with a fleece.
God reduces Gideon's army from 32,000 to 300 so that Israel will not boast. At night they break pitchers, show lamps and blow trumpets, crying "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon".
Gideon pursues the Midianite kings and deals with towns that refused him help. He refuses to be king, but makes an ephod from the gold spoil, and it becomes a snare to Israel.
Gideon's son Abimelech kills his seventy brothers and makes himself king at Shechem. Jotham, the youngest, escapes and tells a parable of trees choosing a king. Abimelech's reign ends in violence.
Two brief notes about judges: Tola of Issachar judges Israel twenty-three years, and Jair of Gilead judges twenty-two years. Jair had thirty sons who rode on thirty ass colts.
Jephthah, an outcast, is called back to lead Gilead against Ammon. Before battle he vows to offer whatever first comes out of his house to meet him, and his daughter comes out with timbrels.
Three brief notes about judges who followed Jephthah: Ibzan of Bethlehem, Elon the Zebulonite and Abdon the Pirathonite.
The angel of the Lord tells Manoah's wife, who is barren, that she will bear a son who is to be a Nazarite from birth and will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
Samson wants to marry a Philistine woman of Timnath. On the way he kills a lion with his bare hands, and at the wedding feast he sets a riddle about honey from its carcass.
Samson's quarrel with the Philistines escalates. He sets foxes with firebrands loose in their corn and kills a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass.

Samson loves Delilah, and the Philistine lords pay her to discover the secret of his strength. When his hair is cut he is captured and blinded. In the temple of Dagon he prays for strength one last time.
In those days there was no king in Israel. A man named Micah sets up idols and hires a Levite as his priest. The tribe of Dan, looking for land, takes both and conquers the city of Laish.

The darkest story in Judges: a Levite's concubine is abused and killed at Gibeah of Benjamin, and the tribes go to war against Benjamin. The book ends, "every man did that which was right in his own eyes."
Naomi loses her husband and two sons in Moab and decides to return to Bethlehem. Her daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her: "whither thou goest, I will go".
Naomi sends Ruth to the threshing floor at night to ask Boaz, a near kinsman, to take her under his protection. Boaz praises her kindness and promises to act.
At the city gate, Boaz settles the matter of redemption with a nearer kinsman and marries Ruth. Their son Obed is the grandfather of David.
Hannah, childless and provoked by her rival, prays at Shiloh so earnestly that Eli thinks she is drunk. She bears Samuel, gives him to serve the Lord, and sings a song of praise.
Eli's sons, priests at Shiloh, treat the offerings of the Lord with contempt. Meanwhile the boy Samuel grows in favour, and a man of God brings word of judgment on Eli's house.
Israel takes the ark of the covenant into battle, but the Philistines win and capture it. Eli's sons are killed, and Eli falls and dies when he hears the news.
The Philistines put the ark in the temple of Dagon, and the idol falls before it. Plagues follow the ark from city to city, until the Philistines send it back on a new cart drawn by two cows.

Samuel calls Israel to put away foreign gods and gathers them at Mizpeh. When the Philistines attack, the Lord thunders against them. Samuel sets up a stone and names it Ebenezer, "hitherto hath the LORD helped us".
Samuel is old and his sons are corrupt, so the elders ask for a king "like all the nations". God tells Samuel that they have rejected him, not Samuel, and Samuel warns them what a king will take.
Saul, a tall young Benjamite, goes looking for his father's lost asses and comes to Samuel. Samuel anoints him privately, and later he is chosen by lot at Mizpeh while hiding among the baggage.
Nahash the Ammonite threatens to put out the right eye of every man in Jabesh-gilead. The Spirit of God comes on Saul, he rallies Israel, and the city is saved. The kingdom is renewed at Gilgal.
Facing a huge Philistine army, Saul's men begin to scatter. When Samuel is late, Saul offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel tells him his kingdom will not continue.
Jonathan and his armourbearer climb up to a Philistine garrison alone, and panic spreads through the enemy camp. Saul's rash oath forbidding food nearly costs Jonathan his life.
Saul is told to destroy Amalek completely, but he spares King Agag and the best of the livestock. Samuel tells him, "to obey is better than sacrifice", and that the Lord has rejected him as king.
God sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint one of Jesse's sons. Seven sons pass before him, but "the LORD looketh on the heart". The youngest, David, is called in from the sheep.
The Spirit of the Lord departs from Saul and an evil spirit troubles him. David, "cunning in playing", is brought to play the harp, and Saul is refreshed.
After Goliath, Jonathan loves David "as his own soul", while Saul grows jealous as the women sing "David his ten thousands". Jonathan warns David with arrows shot in a field, and they part in tears.
On the run, David asks Ahimelech the priest at Nob for bread and is given the hallowed bread and Goliath's sword. In Gath he pretends to be mad to escape King Achish.
David gathers about four hundred men at the cave of Adullam. Doeg the Edomite tells Saul that the priests helped David, and Saul has them killed. Abiathar alone escapes to David.
David asks the Lord and saves the town of Keilah from the Philistines, but must flee when its people would hand him over. Jonathan finds him in the wilderness and strengthens his hand in God.
Saul goes into a cave at En-gedi where David and his men are hiding. David secretly cuts off the skirt of Saul's robe but will not harm "the LORD's anointed". Saul weeps when he learns of it.
David asks the rich and churlish Nabal for provisions and is insulted. David sets out for revenge, but Nabal's wise wife Abigail meets him with gifts and words that turn him back.
David and Abishai creep into Saul's camp at night and take his spear and water jug as he sleeps. Again David refuses to harm Saul, and calls to him from the opposite hill.
Despairing of escaping Saul, David takes refuge with Achish of Gath and is given the town of Ziklag. When the Philistines march against Israel, their lords refuse to let David fight with them.
David returns to find Ziklag burned and the families taken by Amalekites. His men speak of stoning him, but "David encouraged himself in the LORD", pursues the raiders and recovers everything.
With the Philistines gathered and God silent, Saul disguises himself and visits a woman with a familiar spirit at Endor, asking her to bring up Samuel.
An Amalekite brings David news of Saul's death, expecting a reward. David mourns and composes a lament for Saul and Jonathan: "How are the mighty fallen!"
David is anointed king over Judah at Hebron, while Abner makes Saul's son Ish-bosheth king over Israel. Their forces meet at the pool of Gibeon.
A long war follows between the house of Saul and the house of David. Abner changes sides but is killed by Joab, and Ish-bosheth is murdered in his bed. David punishes the murderers.
All the tribes come to David at Hebron and anoint him king over Israel. He is thirty years old and reigns forty years.
David takes the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites, and it becomes the city of David. Hiram, king of Tyre, sends cedar and craftsmen to build David a house.
David defeats the Philistines, Moab, Zobah and Syria, and reigns with justice. He shows kindness to Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth, who eats at the king's table.
At the time when kings go forth to battle, David stays in Jerusalem. He sees Bathsheba bathing, takes her, and when she is with child arranges the death of her husband Uriah in battle.

The prophet Nathan tells David a story of a rich man who took a poor man's only lamb. David is furious, and Nathan says, "Thou art the man." David confesses, and the child dies. Solomon is born afterwards.
David's son Amnon desires his half-sister Tamar, deceives her, forces her, and then hates her. Two years later her brother Absalom has Amnon killed and flees.
Joab sends a wise woman of Tekoah to persuade David, through a story, to bring Absalom home. Absalom returns, but waits two years before he sees the king's face.
Absalom steals the hearts of Israel and proclaims himself king at Hebron. David flees Jerusalem weeping. Hushai, David's friend, defeats the advice of Ahithophel at Absalom's court.
David's army fights Absalom's in the wood of Ephraim. Absalom's head catches in an oak, and Joab kills him against the king's order. David weeps, "O my son Absalom... would God I had died for thee."
Joab rebukes David for mourning while his loyal men feel shamed. David returns to Jerusalem, pardons Shimei who had cursed him, and is met by Mephibosheth and old Barzillai.
Sheba, a Benjamite, calls Israel away from David. Joab kills his rival Amasa and besieges Abel, where a wise woman ends the siege.
As David lies old and frail, his son Adonijah declares himself king. Nathan and Bathsheba remind David of his promise, and Solomon is anointed and rides on the king's mule.
David gives Solomon his final charge to walk in God's ways and dies after reigning forty years. Solomon secures his throne, dealing with Adonijah, Joab and Shimei.
Two women come before Solomon, each claiming the same living baby. He orders a sword to divide the child, and the true mother gives up her claim to save it.
After the temple is finished, God appears to Solomon a second time with a promise and a warning. Solomon gives cities to Hiram and builds up his kingdom.
Solomon loves many foreign women, who turn his heart after other gods in his old age. God tells him the kingdom will be torn from his son, and raises up adversaries, among them Jeroboam.
Jeroboam, king of the northern tribes, fears that his people will return to Jerusalem to worship. He sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan, saying, "behold thy gods, O Israel".
A man of God from Judah cries against Jeroboam's altar at Bethel, and the altar splits. On his way home he is deceived by an old prophet, disobeys God's word, and is killed by a lion.

Jeroboam's son falls sick, and his wife goes in disguise to the blind prophet Ahijah. He recognises her and pronounces judgment on Jeroboam's house. The chapter also records Rehoboam's reign in Judah.
A rapid account of kings in both kingdoms: Abijam and good King Asa in Judah, and in Israel a succession of coups through Baasha, Zimri and Omri to Ahab, who marries Jezebel and serves Baal.
Elijah the Tishbite tells King Ahab there will be no dew or rain but by his word. He hides by the brook Cherith, where ravens bring him bread and flesh.
God sends Elijah to a widow in Zarephath who has only a handful of meal and a little oil. Her barrel of meal and cruse of oil do not run out, and Elijah prays for her son when he dies.

After Carmel, Jezebel threatens Elijah's life and he flees into the wilderness, asking to die. An angel feeds him, and at Horeb God speaks to him not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but in "a still small voice".
Ben-hadad of Syria besieges Samaria, and a prophet promises Ahab victory. Ahab wins twice but lets Ben-hadad go with a treaty, and a prophet rebukes him.
Ahab wants Naboth's vineyard, but Naboth will not sell his family inheritance. Jezebel arranges false witnesses and Naboth is stoned. Elijah meets Ahab in the vineyard with God's judgment.

Ahab and Jehoshaphat plan to retake Ramoth-gilead. Four hundred prophets promise success, but Micaiah foretells disaster. Ahab disguises himself in battle, but an arrow drawn "at a venture" strikes him.
King Ahaziah, injured in a fall, sends to ask Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he will recover. Elijah intercepts the messengers, and fire comes down on the captains sent to arrest him.

Elisha refuses to leave Elijah as they walk from Gilgal to the Jordan. Elijah parts the river with his mantle, a chariot of fire appears, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha takes up the mantle.
The men of Jericho tell Elisha their water is bad. He throws salt into the spring, and the water is healed.
On the road to Bethel, a crowd of youths mocks Elisha, "Go up, thou bald head." He curses them in the name of the Lord, and two she-bears come out of the wood.
Moab rebels against Israel. The kings of Israel, Judah and Edom march against it and run out of water in the wilderness, and Elisha tells them to dig ditches that the Lord will fill.
A prophet's widow is about to lose her two sons to a creditor. Elisha tells her to borrow empty vessels, and her small pot of oil fills every one.
A woman of Shunem makes a room for Elisha, and he promises her a son. Years later the boy dies in her lap, she rides to find Elisha, and he raises the child.
During a famine, wild gourds poison a pot of stew, and Elisha heals it with meal. Then twenty loaves feed a hundred men, with some left over.
While the sons of the prophets cut beams by the Jordan, a borrowed axe head falls into the water. Elisha cuts a stick, throws it in, and the iron swims.
The king of Syria sends an army to capture Elisha at Dothan. Elisha's frightened servant has his eyes opened to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.
Syria besieges Samaria until there is terrible famine. Elisha foretells plenty by the next day, and four lepers discover the Syrian camp deserted.
Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu king of Israel. Jehu, who "driveth furiously", kills Joram and Jezebel, wipes out Ahab's house and destroys the worshippers of Baal.
King Joash visits the dying Elisha, who has him shoot an arrow and strike the ground. Later a dead man thrown into Elisha's tomb revives when he touches Elisha's bones.
Assyria takes Samaria and carries Israel away captive. The chapter explains why, in a long reflection on Israel's turning from God, and tells how Samaria was resettled by other peoples.
Chronicles opens with nine chapters of family lists running from Adam through Israel's tribes to those who returned from exile. Among them is the brief prayer of Jabez.
Chronicles lists David's mighty men, among them the three who broke through the Philistine lines to bring him water from Bethlehem's well, and the men who came to make him king.
David may not build the temple, but he gathers materials, organises the priests, Levites and singers, and gives Solomon the plans. He ends with a prayer: "all things come of thee".
Asa king of Judah removes idols and relies on the Lord against a vast Ethiopian army. The prophet Azariah encourages him, but in later years Asa relies on Syria instead of God.
Jehoshaphat sends teachers of the law through Judah. When a great army comes against him, he prays, "our eyes are upon thee", and sends singers before the army to praise the Lord.
Uzziah becomes king at sixteen and prospers while he seeks God. In his strength he grows proud, enters the temple to burn incense, and is struck with leprosy.
The last kings of Judah do evil, and the people mock God's messengers. Babylon burns the temple and carries the people away. Chronicles ends with Cyrus of Persia telling them to go up and build.
Cyrus king of Persia proclaims that the God of heaven has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem. He returns the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken.
A list of the families who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel, numbering over forty-two thousand, with their servants, singers and animals.
In the seventh month the returned exiles gather in Jerusalem, rebuild the altar on its old place, and keep the feast of tabernacles, though the temple foundation is not yet laid.
When the foundation of the temple is laid, the priests and Levites praise the Lord. Many shout for joy, but old men who had seen the first temple weep aloud.
The people of the land offer to help build, are refused, and then work to frustrate the builders. Letters to the Persian kings bring the work to a stop.
The prophets Haggai and Zechariah stir Zerubbabel and Jeshua to resume building. The governor Tatnai writes to Darius to ask whether Cyrus really allowed it.
Darius finds Cyrus' decree and orders that the work go on at the royal expense. The temple is finished and dedicated with joy, and the Passover is kept.

Ezra, a scribe skilled in the law of Moses, travels from Babylon to Jerusalem with a letter from King Artaxerxes. He is ashamed to ask for soldiers, so the group fasts and prays for protection on the way.
Ezra learns that many, including leaders, have married women of the surrounding peoples. He tears his garments and prays in shame, and the people agree to put away the foreign wives.
Nehemiah, cupbearer to the king of Persia, hears that Jerusalem's wall is broken down and its gates burned. He weeps, fasts and prays for many days.
The king sees Nehemiah's sad face and asks what he wants. Nehemiah prays silently, then asks to be sent to rebuild Jerusalem. He inspects the walls by night.
Families build sections of the wall side by side. Sanballat and Tobiah mock and threaten, so the builders work with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other.
Poor Jews are mortgaging their fields and selling their children to pay debts to their wealthy brothers. Nehemiah is angry, calls an assembly, and has the nobles restore what they took.
Nehemiah's enemies try plots and false reports to stop him, but he answers, "I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down". The wall is finished in fifty-two days.

The people gather and ask Ezra to bring the book of the law. He reads from morning to midday while Levites help them understand, and the people weep. They are told, "the joy of the LORD is your strength."
The people fast, confess their sins, and the Levites lead a long prayer recalling God's faithfulness from creation to the exile. The leaders seal a written covenant to keep God's law.
The wall of Jerusalem is dedicated with two great choirs walking on the wall in opposite directions, "so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even afar off."
On returning from Persia, Nehemiah finds Tobiah living in a temple room, Levites unpaid and the sabbath broken. He sets things right and prays, "Remember me, O my God, for good."
At a great feast, Queen Vashti refuses the king's command to appear, and is removed. A search for a new queen brings Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, to the palace.
Mordecai learns of a plot by two of the king's chamberlains to kill King Ahasuerus. He tells Esther, the plot is foiled, and the deed is written in the king's chronicles.
Haman is promoted, but Mordecai will not bow to him. In his anger Haman obtains a decree, sealed with the king's ring, to destroy all the Jews on a single day.
Esther appears before the king unsummoned, and he holds out the golden sceptre. She invites him and Haman to a banquet. Haman goes home proud and builds a gallows for Mordecai.
On a sleepless night, the king has the chronicles read and learns that Mordecai was never rewarded. Haman, arriving to ask for Mordecai's death, is made to honour him through the streets.
At Esther's second banquet she pleads for her life and her people's, and names Haman as the enemy. Haman is hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai.
A new decree allows the Jews to defend themselves. On the appointed day they overcome their enemies, and Mordecai rises to high honour.
Mordecai and Esther write to the Jews to keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar each year as days of feasting and gladness, called Purim after the "pur", the lot Haman cast.

Job of Uz is perfect and upright, and greatly blessed. Satan says Job serves God only for gain, and Job loses his wealth, his children and his health. Still he says, "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away."
Job curses the day he was born. His three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, insist his suffering must come from sin. Job protests his innocence and longs to plead his case with God.
A younger man, Elihu, angry with Job and with the three friends, speaks at length about how God teaches through suffering and about God's greatness in the storm.
The Lord answers Job out of the whirlwind: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" He questions Job about creation, from the stars to behemoth and leviathan.
Job answers, "now mine eye seeth thee", and repents in dust and ashes. God rebukes the three friends, Job prays for them, and God gives Job twice as much as he had before.
The first psalm contrasts two ways: the blessed man who delights in the law of the Lord and is like a tree planted by rivers of water, and the ungodly, who are like chaff.
According to its heading, David wrote this psalm after Nathan confronted him over Bathsheba. "Have mercy upon me, O God... Create in me a clean heart."
A psalm of trust for those who dwell "in the secret place of the most High": God is refuge and fortress, and his angels keep his people in all their ways.
Bless the LORD, O my soul. This psalm praises God through creation: the light as his garment, the springs and the birds, the cedars, the sea and its creatures, all waiting on him.
Every line of this psalm ends with the same refrain, "for his mercy endureth for ever", as it gives thanks for creation, the exodus and God's care for the lowly.
The longest psalm, 176 verses in 22 sections, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Nearly every verse speaks of God's word: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path."
Wisdom is pictured as a woman crying out in the streets and at the city gates, calling the simple to turn and warning of what comes to those who refuse her.
A father's counsel to his son: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding." It includes honouring God with your wealth and accepting his correction.
Wisdom speaks of being with God before creation, "rejoicing in the habitable part of his earth". Then two women invite the simple: Wisdom to her feast, and the foolish woman to stolen waters.
Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies. An acrostic poem praising a capable, generous woman who fears the Lord.
Vanity of vanities... all is vanity. The Preacher searches for meaning in wisdom, pleasure, work and wealth, and finds them all to be like chasing the wind under the sun.
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven. The Preacher reflects on time, God's work and eternity set in the human heart.
The book ends by urging the young to "remember now thy Creator" before old age, pictured in a poem of a house falling into decay. The conclusion: "Fear God, and keep his commandments."
The Song of Solomon is a love poem between a bride and her beloved. In these chapters they praise each other and long to be together: "his banner over me was love."
The bride searches the city at night for the one her soul loves, and finds him. The chapter ends with a wedding procession of King Solomon.
The beloved praises the bride in images of gardens and spices. She hesitates to open her door at night, then searches for him, describing him to the daughters of Jerusalem.
The poem reaches its climax: "love is strong as death... Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it."
In the year that king Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the Lord on a throne, with seraphims crying "Holy, holy, holy". A live coal touches his lips, and he answers, "Here am I; send me."
Syria and Israel threaten King Ahaz of Judah. Isaiah urges him to trust God and gives a sign: "a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." Matthew 1:23 quotes it.
The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light... For unto us a child is born. The child is named Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
A rod shall come out of the stem of Jesse, a ruler on whom the Spirit of the Lord rests. Under his reign "the wolf also shall dwell with the lamb", and the scattered people are gathered.
A song about the servant of the Lord who is "despised and rejected of men... wounded for our transgressions". The New Testament applies it to Jesus, for example in Acts 8.
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters. God invites the people to come freely, to seek him while he may be found, and promises that his word will not return void.
The book of Isaiah closes with God's promise to create new heavens and a new earth, where weeping is heard no more and "the wolf and the lamb shall feed together".
God calls Jeremiah, who protests that he is a child. God touches his mouth and shows him an almond rod and a boiling pot, and sends him "to root out... to build, and to plant".
Jeremiah stands at the temple gate and warns the people not to trust in "the temple of the LORD" while they oppress the poor and follow other gods. He reminds them of what happened to Shiloh.
God sends Jeremiah to watch a potter at his wheel. When a vessel is marred, the potter makes it again: "as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel."
Jeremiah takes an earthen bottle to the valley of the son of Hinnom, proclaims judgment on Jerusalem, and breaks the bottle before the elders as a sign.
Pashur the priest has Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks. Jeremiah complains bitterly to God, yet says God's word is "as a burning fire shut up in my bones".
Jeremiah's prophecies are written on a scroll by Baruch and read to King Jehoiakim. The king cuts it up with a penknife and burns it piece by piece, and Jeremiah has it written again.
Comfort ye, comfort ye my people. A voice cries to prepare the way of the Lord in the wilderness, all flesh is grass, and those who wait upon the Lord "shall mount up with wings as eagles".
During the Babylonian siege, Jeremiah is arrested as a deserter and later let down into a muddy cistern. An Ethiopian named Ebed-melech rescues him, and King Zedekiah consults him secretly.
After the fall of Jerusalem, Babylon appoints Gedaliah governor over those left in Judah, and Jeremiah stays with him. Ishmael son of Nethaniah murders Gedaliah at Mizpah.
The remnant asks Jeremiah to seek God's will and promises to obey. When God tells them to stay in Judah, they go to Egypt anyway and take Jeremiah with them.
God promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah, not like the one they broke: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts." Hebrews 8 quotes this passage.
Lamentations mourns the fall of Jerusalem in five poems. The first two picture the city as a widow weeping in the night and describe the Lord's anger against Zion.
In the middle of the book's grief comes its turning point: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed... they are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."
The last poems describe the siege's horrors and the people's shame, and end with a prayer: "Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned."

By the river Chebar in Babylon, the exiled priest Ezekiel sees a storm, four living creatures, wheels full of eyes, and above them a throne with "the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD".
God sends Ezekiel to a rebellious house, whether they hear or not. He eats a scroll that tastes as sweet as honey and is made a watchman for Israel.
Ezekiel acts out the coming siege of Jerusalem: he draws the city on a tile, lies on his side for many days, eats rationed bread, and shaves his head and divides the hair.
In a vision Ezekiel is taken to Jerusalem and shown idolatry in the temple itself. He watches the glory of the Lord leave the temple and stand over the mount east of the city.
Ezekiel packs his belongings by day, digs through a wall at night and leaves with his face covered, as a sign of the coming exile of Jerusalem's king and people.
God again makes Ezekiel a watchman who must warn the wicked. "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live." News arrives that Jerusalem has fallen.
God condemns the shepherds of Israel, who fed themselves instead of the flock. He promises, "I will both search my sheep, and seek them out," and to set one shepherd over them, "my servant David".
Ezekiel joins two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, into one in his hand, a sign that God will make the divided people one nation under one king.
Ezekiel prophesies against Gog of the land of Magog, who leads many nations against restored Israel in the latter days and is defeated by God.
In the last nine chapters, Ezekiel is shown a new temple with careful measurements. The glory of the Lord returns, a river flows from the temple, and the city is named "The LORD is there".

Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah are taken to Babylon to be trained for the king's service. Daniel asks to eat pulse and drink water instead of the king's meat, and after ten days they look healthier.
Nebuchadnezzar demands that his wise men tell him his dream as well as its meaning. Daniel and his friends pray, and God reveals the great image of gold, silver, brass, iron and clay.

Nebuchadnezzar tells, in his own words, of a dream of a great tree cut down. Daniel interprets it, the proud king is driven out to live like a beast, and when his understanding returns he praises the God of heaven.
Daniel dreams of four great beasts rising from the sea, and of the Ancient of days on his throne. One "like the Son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven and is given an everlasting kingdom.
Daniel sees a ram with two horns and a goat with one great horn. The angel Gabriel explains that they stand for the kings of Media and Persia and of Grecia.
Reading Jeremiah's prophecy of seventy years, Daniel confesses his people's sins and prays for Jerusalem. Gabriel comes to him with a prophecy of seventy weeks.

By the river Hiddekel, Daniel sees a man clothed in linen, and is told of conflicts between kings to come. The book ends with a promise of resurrection: "many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake."
God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, who is unfaithful to him, and their children's names carry messages to Israel. Hosea buys her back, a picture of God's love for unfaithful Israel.
God charges Israel with forgetting him, yet cannot give them up: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt." The book ends with a call to return.
A plague of locusts strips the land. Joel calls the people to mourn and fast: "rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God."
God promises to restore "the years that the locust hath eaten", and afterwards, "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh." Peter quotes this at Pentecost in Acts 2.
God gathers the nations for judgment in the valley of Jehoshaphat, "multitudes in the valley of decision", while promising to be the hope of his people.
Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa, pronounces judgment on Israel's neighbours "for three transgressions... and for four", and then turns to Judah and Israel themselves.
Amos condemns Israel's luxury and oppression of the poor, and empty worship: "let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream."
Amos sees locusts, fire, a plumbline and a basket of summer fruit. The priest of Bethel tells him to go home, and the book ends with a promise to raise up the fallen tabernacle of David.
The shortest book in the Old Testament, a single chapter, announces judgment on Edom for its pride and its violence against Judah, and ends, "the kingdom shall be the LORD's."
From inside the fish, Jonah prays a psalm of distress and thanksgiving: "Salvation is of the LORD." The Lord speaks to the fish, and it brings Jonah up onto dry land.
The word of the Lord comes to Jonah a second time, and he preaches in Nineveh, "Yet forty days". The people and the king believe God, fast and put on sackcloth, and God spares the city.
Jonah is angry that God spared Nineveh. God prepares a gourd to shade him and then a worm to destroy it, and asks whether he should not spare the great city with its people and cattle.
Micah announces judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem, and rebukes rulers who "hate the good, and love the evil" and prophets who preach for money.
But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little... yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel. Matthew 2 quotes this prophecy.
God brings a case against his people and recalls his kindness. What does he require? "To do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God."
Micah grieves over a society without trust, yet says, "I will look unto the LORD." The book ends praising God who "delighteth in mercy" and will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
Nahum announces the fall of Nineveh, capital of Assyria, about a century after Jonah. "The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power", and a stronghold to those who trust him.
Habakkuk asks God how long violence will go unpunished. God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans (Babylonians), and Habakkuk asks how a holy God can use a nation even more wicked.
Habakkuk waits on his watchtower for God's answer: write the vision plainly, and "the just shall live by his faith". Paul quotes this line in Romans and Galatians.
Habakkuk's closing prayer remembers God's mighty acts, and ends in trust: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom... Yet I will rejoice in the LORD."
Zephaniah warns of the great day of the Lord coming on Judah and the nations, then promises a humble remnant: "he will rejoice over thee with joy... he will joy over thee with singing."
Haggai rebukes the returned exiles for living in panelled houses while God's house lies waste: "Consider your ways." Zerubbabel, Joshua and the people obey and begin to work.
To those who think the new temple is as nothing compared with Solomon's, God promises, "The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former."

Zechariah sees eight visions in one night: horsemen among myrtle trees, horns and smiths, a measuring line, a golden lampstand with olive trees ("Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit"), a flying scroll and four chariots.
Zechariah sees Joshua the high priest standing in filthy garments with Satan accusing him. The Lord rebukes Satan, Joshua is clothed in clean garments, and a servant called the BRANCH is promised.
Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion... behold, thy King cometh unto thee... lowly, and riding upon an ass. The Gospels quote this at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem.
Zechariah acts as a shepherd paid thirty pieces of silver, which he casts to the potter. God will open a fountain for sin, and "smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered."
The day of the Lord: the nations gather against Jerusalem, the Lord's feet stand on the mount of Olives, living waters flow from Jerusalem, and "the LORD shall be king over all the earth".
I have loved you, saith the LORD. Malachi rebukes priests who offer blemished animals, and husbands who deal treacherously with the wives of their youth.

God will send his messenger to prepare the way, and the Lord will come to his temple "like a refiner's fire". The people are told to bring the whole tithe and see if he will not open the windows of heaven.
The Old Testament closes: "unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings." God promises to send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the Lord.
Warned in a dream, Joseph takes Mary and the child to Egypt. Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem. After Herod's death the family returns and settles in Nazareth.
Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sees Simon Peter and Andrew casting a net, and James and John mending theirs. "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men," and they leave their nets.
After the Sermon on the Mount a leper comes to Jesus: "Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Jesus touches him and says, "I will; be thou clean."
A Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his paralysed servant, but says Jesus need only speak the word. Jesus marvels: "I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel."
Jesus names his twelve apostles and sends them out to the lost sheep of Israel, to preach and heal. He warns them of persecution and tells them not to fear.
John the Baptist, in prison, sends disciples to ask Jesus, "Art thou he that should come?" Jesus points to what they see and hear, and then speaks of John's greatness.

The Pharisees object when Jesus' disciples pluck ears of corn on the sabbath, and when Jesus heals a man with a withered hand in the synagogue. Jesus says "the Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath day."
An enemy sows tares among a farmer's wheat. The servants want to pull them up, but the householder says to let both grow until the harvest. Jesus later explains the parable to his disciples.
Two short parables of the kingdom of heaven: a tiny mustard seed that grows into a tree where birds lodge, and leaven hidden in meal until all is leavened.
Two very short parables: a man finds treasure hidden in a field and sells everything to buy the field, and a merchant sells everything for one pearl of great price.
The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea that gathers fish of every kind. The fishermen keep the good and throw the bad away, and so it will be at the end of the world.
Herod the tetrarch, hearing of Jesus, thinks John the Baptist has risen from the dead. Matthew then tells how Herod had John imprisoned and beheaded at the request of Herodias's daughter.
In the region of Tyre and Sidon, a Canaanite woman begs Jesus to heal her daughter. Jesus at first does not answer, but her persistent reply leads him to say, "O woman, great is thy faith."
After three days with Jesus in a remote place, a crowd has nothing to eat. With seven loaves and a few small fishes, Jesus feeds four thousand men, and seven baskets are left over.
Collectors of the temple tax ask Peter whether his master pays it. Jesus sends Peter to catch a fish, and in its mouth he finds a coin to pay for them both.
Peter asks how often he should forgive, "till seven times?" Jesus answers "until seventy times seven", and tells of a servant forgiven a huge debt who will not forgive a small one.
A householder hires labourers for his vineyard at different hours of the day and pays them all the same wage. Those hired first complain. "So the last shall be first, and the first last."
On his way into Jerusalem, Jesus finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit, and it withers. He tells his amazed disciples about faith and prayer.
A father asks his two sons to work in his vineyard. One refuses but later goes; the other says he will go but does not. Jesus asks the chief priests and elders which one did his father's will.
A householder lets out his vineyard, but the husbandmen beat and kill the servants he sends, and finally his son. Jesus quotes the psalm, "The stone which the builders rejected".
A king prepares a marriage feast for his son, but the invited guests make light of it. He sends his servants to invite everyone they find, good and bad, and one guest has no wedding garment.
A lawyer asks Jesus which is the great commandment. Jesus answers with love for God with all your heart, soul and mind, and love for your neighbour as yourself.
Jesus warns against the scribes and Pharisees, who "say, and do not", and pronounces a series of woes on their hypocrisy. He ends by lamenting over Jerusalem.

On the mount of Olives the disciples ask about the end of the age. Jesus speaks of wars, the destruction of the temple, the coming of the Son of man, and the need to watch, with parables of readiness.
Ten virgins wait with lamps for the bridegroom. Five wise ones bring extra oil and five foolish ones do not. When he comes at midnight, only the ready go in to the marriage.
A man going abroad entrusts his servants with talents, a large sum of money. Two trade and double theirs; the third hides his in the earth. "Well done, thou good and faithful servant."

When the Son of man comes in his glory, he separates the nations as a shepherd divides sheep from goats. "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."
When Judas sees Jesus condemned, he returns the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and hangs himself. The priests use the money to buy the potter's field.

Mark opens fast: John baptizes in the wilderness, Jesus is baptized and tempted, calls fishermen to follow him, and heals many in Capernaum, from a man with an unclean spirit to Peter's mother-in-law.
A parable found only in Mark: a man scatters seed, and it springs up and grows "he knoweth not how", first the blade, then the ear, then the full corn.
Jesus teaches in the synagogue of his home town, but the people take offence: "Is not this the carpenter?" He says a prophet is not without honour except in his own country.
