In the region of Decapolis, people bring Jesus a deaf man with a speech impediment. Jesus takes him aside, touches his ears and tongue and says, "Ephphatha, that is, Be opened."
At Bethsaida, Jesus leads a blind man out of town and heals him in two stages. At first he sees "men as trees, walking", then he sees every man clearly.
Coming down from the mount of the Transfiguration, Jesus finds his disciples unable to heal a boy with a spirit. The father cries, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."
Jesus watches people giving at the temple treasury. A poor widow puts in two mites, and Jesus says she has given more than all the rich, for she gave all she had.
The priest Zacharias is burning incense in the temple when the angel Gabriel tells him that his elderly wife Elisabeth will bear a son, John. Zacharias doubts and is struck dumb.
Mary visits her cousin Elisabeth, and the baby leaps in Elisabeth's womb. Mary responds with a song of praise: "My soul doth magnify the Lord."
Elisabeth gives birth, and the neighbours expect the boy to be named after his father. Zacharias writes "His name is John", his tongue is loosed, and he prophesies.
Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the temple. The aged Simeon takes him in his arms and blesses God, and the prophetess Anna gives thanks.
At twelve, Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem after the Passover. His parents find him after three days in the temple among the teachers: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"
In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus reads from Isaiah, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me", and says, "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." The listeners turn against him.
Jesus teaches from Simon's boat, then tells him to let down his nets. After a night of catching nothing, the nets break with fish. Simon falls at his knees, and Jesus calls him to catch men.
At the gate of Nain, Jesus meets a funeral procession for a widow's only son. He has compassion on her, touches the bier, and says, "Young man, I say unto thee, Arise."
At a Pharisee's house, a woman known as a sinner washes Jesus' feet with her tears and anoints them. Jesus tells a parable of two debtors and says, "Thy sins are forgiven."
A short note that several women travelled with Jesus and the twelve, among them Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, and supported them from their own means.
Martha welcomes Jesus into her house and is busy with serving, while her sister Mary sits at his feet listening. Jesus says "Mary hath chosen that good part".
After teaching the Lord's Prayer, Jesus tells of a friend who knocks at midnight asking for bread. "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find."

A man asks Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute. Jesus warns against covetousness and tells of a rich man who builds bigger barns, but God says, "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee."
A man finds no fruit on his fig tree for three years and wants it cut down. The dresser of the vineyard asks for one more year to dig around it and fertilise it.
On the sabbath, Jesus heals a woman who had been bowed together for eighteen years. The ruler of the synagogue is indignant, and Jesus answers him.
A man makes a great supper, but the invited guests all make excuses. He sends his servant to bring in the poor, the maimed, the lame and the blind, and then to the highways and hedges.
A woman with ten pieces of silver loses one. She lights a candle and sweeps the house until she finds it, then calls her friends to rejoice. So there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.
A steward about to be dismissed reduces his master's debtors' bills to win friends for later, and his master commends his shrewdness. Jesus ends, "Ye cannot serve God and mammon."
A rich man lives in luxury while Lazarus, a beggar covered with sores, lies at his gate. After death their places are reversed, and Abraham speaks of a great gulf fixed between them.
Ten lepers call to Jesus from a distance, and he sends them to show themselves to the priests. On the way they are healed, but only one, a Samaritan, returns to give thanks.
A parable about praying and not giving up: a widow keeps coming to an unjust judge until he grants her justice, simply because she will not stop.
Two men go up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee thanks God he is not like other men; the publican stands far off and says, "God be merciful to me a sinner."
As Jesus nears Jerusalem, he tells of a nobleman who gives ten servants a pound each before travelling to receive a kingdom, and on his return asks what they have gained.
As Jesus comes near Jerusalem and sees the city, he weeps over it, because it did not know the things that belong to its peace, and foretells its destruction.
Pilate, learning that Jesus is from Galilee, sends him to Herod. Herod hopes to see a miracle, but Jesus answers nothing. Herod mocks him and sends him back to Pilate.
Luke's Gospel ends at Bethany. Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his disciples, and is carried up into heaven. They return to Jerusalem with great joy.
John begins, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Word is the light of men, and "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us".
Priests and Levites ask John the Baptist who he is. He says he is not the Christ but a voice crying in the wilderness. The next day he sees Jesus and says, "Behold the Lamb of God."
Andrew and another disciple follow Jesus, and Andrew brings his brother Simon. Philip finds Nathanael, who asks, "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" Philip answers, "Come and see."
At a Passover early in his ministry, Jesus drives the traders out of the temple with a scourge of small cords. Asked for a sign, he says, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up."
A nobleman from Capernaum begs Jesus at Cana to come before his son dies. Jesus says, "Go thy way; thy son liveth," and the man believes. His servants meet him with the news.
At the pool of Bethesda lies a man who has been ill for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks, "Wilt thou be made whole?" and tells him to take up his bed and walk. It is the sabbath.
The day after the feeding of the five thousand, the crowds seek Jesus. He tells them, "I am the bread of life." Many disciples leave him, and Peter says, "Lord, to whom shall we go?"

Jesus goes up to Jerusalem quietly for the feast of tabernacles, then teaches openly in the temple. On the last day he cries, "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink." Opinions about him divide.

The scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery to test Jesus. He writes on the ground and says, "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone." The oldest manuscripts of John do not include this passage; the KJV does.
In the temple treasury Jesus says, "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness." The Pharisees challenge his witness.
Jesus heals a man blind from birth with clay and the pool of Siloam. The Pharisees question the man and his parents, and he answers, "one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see."
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. Jesus speaks of the sheepfold, the door, and the sheep who know their shepherd's voice.

On his last night, after washing the disciples' feet, Jesus speaks to them at length: "Let not your heart be troubled", "I am the way, the truth, and the life", "I am the true vine", and the promise of the Comforter.
Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays for himself, for his disciples, and for all who will believe through their word, "that they all may be one".
By the Sea of Tiberias the disciples fish all night and catch nothing. A man on the shore tells them to cast on the right side, the net fills with 153 great fish, and John says, "It is the Lord."

Acts opens with the risen Jesus telling the apostles they will be his witnesses "unto the uttermost part of the earth" and being taken up in a cloud. The apostles then choose Matthias to replace Judas.
At the temple gate called Beautiful, a man lame from birth asks Peter and John for money. Peter says, "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee," and the man walks and leaps.
Peter and John are arrested and questioned by the council. Peter, filled with the Holy Ghost, speaks boldly, and the rulers marvel that these "unlearned and ignorant men" had been with Jesus.
The believers are of one heart and soul, and no one says that anything he owns is his own. Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet.
Ananias and his wife Sapphira sell land and keep back part of the price while claiming to give it all. Peter says they have lied to the Holy Ghost, and both fall down dead.
The apostles are jailed, but an angel opens the prison doors at night. Brought before the council, they say "We ought to obey God rather than men." Gamaliel urges caution.
The Greek-speaking widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution. The apostles have the disciples choose seven men full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, among them Stephen and Philip.

Stephen is accused before the council and answers with a long account of Israel's history. Seeing heaven opened, he is stoned, praying "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." A young man named Saul looks on.
Persecution scatters the believers. Philip preaches Christ in Samaria with signs, and Simon the sorcerer believes but later tries to buy the power to give the Holy Ghost.

An angel sends Philip to the desert road toward Gaza, where an Ethiopian official is reading Isaiah in his chariot. "Understandest thou what thou readest?" Philip explains the passage and baptizes him.
At Lydda, Peter heals Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years. At Joppa a disciple called Tabitha (Dorcas), known for her good works, dies, and Peter prays and says, "Tabitha, arise."

A Roman centurion named Cornelius sees an angel, while Peter sees a sheet of animals and hears, "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common." Peter preaches in Cornelius's house and the Holy Ghost falls on the Gentiles.

Scattered believers preach to Greeks at Antioch, and many believe. Barnabas brings Saul there to teach, and "the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch". They send relief to Judaea in a famine.

Herod kills James the brother of John and imprisons Peter. On the night before his trial an angel wakes Peter, his chains fall off, and he knocks at Mary's house, where a girl named Rhoda is too glad to open the gate.
The church at Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul, now called Paul, to Cyprus and on to the cities of Galatia. They preach in synagogues, turn to the Gentiles, and face welcome and stoning.
Some teach that Gentile believers must be circumcised. The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem, Peter and James speak, and a letter goes out asking the Gentiles only to keep a few necessary things.
Paul and Barnabas plan to revisit the churches, but disagree sharply over taking John Mark. Barnabas sails with Mark to Cyprus, and Paul chooses Silas.
At Lystra, Paul meets a young disciple named Timothy, whose mother was Jewish and father Greek, and takes him along. The churches are "established in the faith, and increased in number daily."
Kept by the Holy Ghost from preaching in Asia and Bithynia, Paul sees a vision at night of a man of Macedonia: "Come over into Macedonia, and help us." The narrative switches to "we".
At Philippi, Paul speaks to women at a riverside place of prayer. Lydia, a seller of purple cloth from Thyatira, listens, "whose heart the Lord opened", and her household is baptized.

Paul casts out a spirit from a slave girl, and her owners have Paul and Silas beaten and jailed. At midnight they sing praises, an earthquake opens the doors, and the jailer asks, "what must I do to be saved?"
In Thessalonica, Paul reasons from the scriptures and some believe, but a mob forms. In Berea the Jews "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so."
Paul is troubled by the city's idols. Brought to the Areopagus, he speaks of an altar "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD" and of the God in whom "we live, and move, and have our being."

Paul works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth. In a vision the Lord tells him not to be afraid, and he stays eighteen months. The proconsul Gallio refuses to hear the case against him.
Apollos, an eloquent man from Alexandria, teaches about Jesus at Ephesus but knows only John's baptism. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain "the way of God more perfectly."
Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years. God works special miracles through him, the seven sons of Sceva are overpowered by an evil spirit, and those who practised magic burn their books.

Demetrius, a silversmith who makes shrines of Diana, stirs up the craftsmen against Paul. The crowd fills the theatre shouting "Great is Diana of the Ephesians" for two hours until the town clerk calms them.
At Troas, Paul talks until midnight, and a young man named Eutychus falls asleep in a window and falls from the third storey. Paul embraces him and says, "his life is in him."
At Miletus, Paul says goodbye to the elders of Ephesus. He reminds them how he served, warns of wolves among the flock, and quotes Jesus: "It is more blessed to give than to receive."
On the way to Jerusalem, the prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul's girdle (belt) as a sign of what awaits Paul. Paul says he is ready to die for the name of the Lord Jesus.

Paul is seized in the temple, accused of bringing Greeks inside. Rescued by Roman soldiers, he tells the crowd the story of his conversion, claims his Roman citizenship, and stands before the council.
More than forty men swear not to eat until they have killed Paul. His sister's son hears of the plot, and the chief captain sends Paul by night under heavy guard to the governor Felix at Caesarea.
The high priest's lawyer Tertullus accuses Paul before Felix. Paul answers the charges. Felix listens to him on righteousness and judgment, trembles, and keeps Paul in prison for two years.
Before the new governor Festus, Paul appeals to Caesar. He then tells King Agrippa his story, and Agrippa says, "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian."
Sailing for Rome as a prisoner, Paul's ship is caught in a great storm for many days. An angel promises that no one will be lost, and all 276 aboard reach land when the ship runs aground.
On Malta a viper fastens on Paul's hand as he gathers sticks. He shakes it into the fire unharmed. He heals the father of Publius, the island's chief man, and others who are sick.
Believers come out to meet Paul on the road to Rome. He lives two years in his own hired house under guard, receiving all who come and preaching the kingdom of God, and Acts ends there.
Paul opens his letter to Rome: he is "not ashamed of the gospel". He argues that Gentiles and Jews alike are under sin: "all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."

Paul explains being justified freely by God's grace through faith in Christ. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness, and "we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ."

Paul writes of being buried with Christ in baptism and raised to new life, the struggle with sin in chapter 7, and life in the Spirit: "There is therefore now no condemnation" and "nothing shall be able to separate us from the love of God."

Paul grieves for his own people Israel and asks whether God has cast them away. He answers no, uses the picture of an olive tree with grafted branches, and ends in praise: "O the depth of the riches".
Paul urges the Romans to "present your bodies a living sacrifice". He writes about gifts in one body, love without hypocrisy, the governing authorities, and receiving one another despite differences.
The church at Corinth is split into factions: "I am of Paul; and I of Apollos". Paul answers with "Christ crucified", the wisdom of God that looks like foolishness to the world.
Paul tells the Corinthians to deal with a case of serious sexual sin in the church, rebukes believers who take each other to court, and says, "ye are not your own... ye are bought with a price."
Paul answers questions the Corinthians had written to him about marriage, divorce, remaining single, and staying in the condition in which one was called.
Paul lists the witnesses who saw the risen Christ and argues that if Christ is not raised, faith is vain. He ends with the resurrection of the dead: "O death, where is thy sting?"

Paul begins his second letter to Corinth by blessing "the God of all comfort", who comforts us so that we can comfort others, and tells of a recent trouble in Asia so heavy that "we despaired even of life."
Paul explains why he wrote his earlier sorrowful letter, and urges the church to forgive and comfort the one who caused grief, "Lest Satan should get an advantage of us."

We have this treasure in earthen vessels. Paul describes being troubled but not distressed, perplexed but not in despair, and says, "the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal."
Paul encourages the Corinthians to complete their collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, pointing to the generous churches of Macedonia: "God loveth a cheerful giver."
Paul tells of a man caught up to the third heaven and of his own "thorn in the flesh". The Lord's answer is "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
Paul tells the Galatians that his gospel came by revelation of Jesus Christ, not from men. He recounts his past and his meetings with the apostles, and how he withstood Peter at Antioch.

O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you? Paul argues from Abraham that the promise comes by faith, the law was a schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, and believers are sons and heirs. He ends with an allegory of Hagar and Sarah.

Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free. Paul contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit, "love, joy, peace", and urges bearing one another's burdens.
Paul's letter to Ephesus opens with one long blessing of God for choosing, redeeming and sealing his people in Christ, and a prayer that they may know "the hope of his calling".

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God. Paul tells Gentile readers that Christ has broken down the middle wall of partition between them and Israel.

Paul urges the Ephesians to keep "the unity of the Spirit": one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith. Christ gives gifts to build up the body, and believers are to put off the old man and put on the new.

Put on the whole armour of God. Paul describes the believer's struggle against spiritual powers using a soldier's equipment: the girdle (belt) of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit.
Writing from prison, Paul tells the Philippians that his chains have helped spread the gospel. "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain."
Paul urges humility and quotes or composes a passage on Christ, who "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant", and whom God has highly exalted.

Paul counts his past advantages as loss "for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus". Not yet perfect, he says, "I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."
Rejoice in the Lord alway. Paul writes of prayer and "the peace of God, which passeth all understanding", of learning to be content in every state, and thanks the Philippians for their gift.

Paul writes to the Colossians of the Son, "the image of the invisible God", by whom all things were created and in whom "all things consist" (hold together), and through whom God reconciles all things.
Set your affection on things above. Paul tells the Colossians that their life is hid with Christ in God, lists what to put off and what to put on, and gives instructions for households.
Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians' "work of faith, and labour of love, and patience of hope", recalls his time with them, and rejoices at Timothy's report that they are standing firm.
Paul comforts the Thessalonians about believers who have died: the dead in Christ shall rise first, and "so shall we ever be with the Lord." The day of the Lord comes as a thief in the night.
Paul encourages the persecuted Thessalonians and corrects the claim that the day of Christ has already come, saying a falling away and "that man of sin" must come first.
Paul asks for prayer and warns against idleness. He reminds them that he worked for his own bread, and says, "if any would not work, neither should he eat."
Paul charges Timothy at Ephesus to oppose false teaching, recalls the mercy shown to himself as "chief" of sinners, and gives the qualifications for bishops and deacons.

Paul tells Timothy, "Let no man despise thy youth", gives counsel on caring for widows and elders, and warns that "the love of money is the root of all evil." He urges him to "fight the good fight of faith."
In what may be his last letter, Paul remembers Timothy's faith, which first lived in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and tells him to stir up the gift of God and not be ashamed.
Paul tells Timothy to commit what he has learned to faithful men who can teach others, to endure hardness "as a good soldier", and to be "a workman that needeth not to be ashamed".
Paul warns of perilous times and reminds Timothy that "All scripture is given by inspiration of God". He ends, "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith."
Paul left Titus in Crete to appoint elders in every city. He lists their qualifications and warns about unruly talkers and deceivers.

Paul tells Titus what to teach older and younger men and women and servants. "The grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men", teaching believers to be careful to maintain good works.

A short personal letter. Paul writes to Philemon about Onesimus, a runaway servant who has become a believer, and asks Philemon to receive him "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved."
Hebrews begins, "God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake... hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son." The Son is greater than the angels and than Moses.
We have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities. Hebrews compares Jesus to Melchisedec, a priest-king who blessed Abraham.
Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's new covenant and compares the tabernacle sacrifices with Christ's single offering, then urges readers to draw near "with a true heart in full assurance of faith".
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. Hebrews 11 lists those who lived by faith, from Abel, Enoch and Noah to Abraham, Moses, Rahab and many more.

Seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses... let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus. Hebrews speaks of the Lord's discipline as a father's.

James begins, "count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations (trials)", and tells readers to ask God for wisdom, to be "swift to hear, slow to speak", and to be "doers of the word, and not hearers only."
James warns against favouring the rich over the poor, and asks what good faith is without works: "faith without works is dead." He points to Abraham and Rahab.
James warns that the tongue is a small member that boasts great things: "Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!" He contrasts earthly wisdom with "the wisdom that is from above".

James warns the oppressive rich, urges patience until the coming of the Lord, and speaks of praying for the sick: "The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much", as Elijah's prayers did.
Peter writes to scattered believers of "a lively (living) hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ". Their faith is tried like gold, and they are "a chosen generation, a royal priesthood".
Peter speaks of wives and husbands, of being ready "to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you", and of not thinking the "fiery trial" strange.

Peter tells the elders to "Feed the flock of God", and all to be clothed with humility, "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you." He warns that the devil walks about "as a roaring lion".
Peter lists qualities to add to faith, from virtue to charity (love), and says he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty on the holy mount. No prophecy of scripture came "by the will of man".
Peter warns that false teachers will come in among believers, and recalls God's judgments on the fallen angels, the ancient world and Sodom, while he rescued Noah and Lot.

Scoffers ask "Where is the promise of his coming?" Peter answers that "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years", that the Lord is not slack but longsuffering, and the day of the Lord will come as a thief.
John writes of what he has seen and heard of the Word of life. "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all." If we confess our sins, he is faithful to forgive. He warns of antichrists.
Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us. John tells readers to test the spirits and to love one another, for "God is love" and "There is no fear in love".
John writes "that ye may know that ye have eternal life". Faith overcomes the world, and "He that hath the Son hath life". The letter ends, "keep yourselves from idols."
A one-chapter letter from "the elder" to "the elect lady and her children", urging them to walk in truth and love, and not to welcome those who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
A short letter from the elder to Gaius, praising his hospitality to travelling believers, criticising Diotrephes, "who loveth to have the preeminence", and commending Demetrius.

Jude urges readers to "earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints", warns against ungodly men who have crept in, and ends with a famous doxology: "Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling".

On the isle of Patmos, John hears a great voice "on the Lord's day" and turns to see one like the Son of man among seven golden candlesticks, his face shining like the sun. He is told to write what he sees.
Christ sends a message to each of seven churches in Asia, from Ephesus to Laodicea, with praise, rebuke and promises "to him that overcometh". "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock."
John sees a door opened in heaven and a throne with one sitting on it, surrounded by a rainbow, twenty-four elders and four living creatures who cry, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty".
No one is found worthy to open a sealed book, until John sees "a Lamb as it had been slain". All heaven sings a new song: "Worthy is the Lamb that was slain".

The Lamb opens the seals one by one: four horsemen, the souls of martyrs, a great earthquake, and 144,000 sealed from Israel with a great multitude no one can number. The seventh seal brings silence in heaven.

Seven angels sound trumpets, bringing hail and fire, a burning mountain, a falling star, darkness and woes. John eats a little book, and two witnesses prophesy. At the seventh trumpet, "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord".
John sees a woman clothed with the sun giving birth to a child, and a great red dragon waiting to devour him. There is war in heaven, and the dragon, "that old serpent", is cast out.
A beast rises from the sea and receives power from the dragon, and another beast rises from the earth and makes people receive a mark. "Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast".
The Lamb stands on mount Sion with the 144,000. Three angels fly through heaven with an everlasting gospel and warnings, and the earth is reaped like a harvest.
Seven angels pour out seven vials (bowls) of the wrath of God on the earth, the sea, the rivers, the sun, the throne of the beast and the Euphrates, ending with "It is done."
John sees a woman called "Babylon the great" riding a scarlet beast. An angel announces her fall, and kings, merchants and sailors lament as the great city is thrown down.
A great multitude in heaven cries "Alleluia" over Babylon's judgment and announces "the marriage of the Lamb". "Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb."

Heaven opens and a rider on a white horse appears, called Faithful and True and "The Word of God", with "KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS" written on his vesture. The beast and the false prophet are defeated.
Satan is bound for a thousand years, and martyrs reign with Christ. After a last rebellion, the devil is cast into the lake of fire, and the dead are judged before a great white throne.
John sees "a new heaven and a new earth" and the holy city coming down from God. "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death". "Behold, I make all things new."
An angel shows John the holy Jerusalem, with gates of pearl and a street of gold. There is no temple in it, "for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it", and no need of the sun.

The Bible's last chapter shows a pure river of water of life and the tree of life. "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come." Jesus says, "Surely I come quickly," and John answers, "Even so, come, Lord Jesus."

After King Jeconiah is carried to Babylon, Jeremiah is shown two baskets of figs, one very good and one very bad. The good figs stand for the exiles God will bring back; the bad for Zedekiah and those left behind.

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, Jeremiah warns that the land will serve the king of Babylon seventy years, and then Babylon itself will be judged. He is told to make the nations drink the cup of God's fury.
